Text: DESIGN OF PIPING SYSTEMS  ![Fig. A.2 Configuration in the y-plane.](figures/MWK_1956_p0306_fig01_fig-a-2-configuration-in-the-y-plane.png)  The integration limits are from the point of load application (lower limit) to the fixed end, or to the point where the loading is discontinuous. Thus, the limits for the moments and forces applied at the free end are from $A$ to $O'$. For the uniform load, two sets of limits are needed, $F$ to $N$, and $N$ to $O'$, since the load application begins at $F$, accumulates linearly to $N$, and then acts with constant effect to $O'$.  By inspection of the integrals it is seen that they all are functions of the following basic expressions called shape coefficients:  $$s = \int kQ \, dl$$  $$u = \int (k \cos^2 \psi + 1.3 \sin^2 \psi) Q \, dl$$  $$v = \int (1.3 \cos^2 \psi + k \sin^2 \psi) Q \, dl \quad (A.5)$$  $$p = \int (1.3 - k) \sin \psi \cos \psi Q \, dl$$  These expressions are conveniently employed in deriving a further series of constants also termed shape coefficients. With reference to concentrated loads these are:  $$s_x = \int x s \, ds \qquad u_x = \int x \, du = \int y \, dq$$  $$s_{xx} = \int x^2 \, ds \qquad u_{xx} = \int x^2 \, du = \int xy \, dq$$  $$s_y = \int y \, ds \qquad v_x = \int y \, dv = \int x \, dq \quad (A.5)$$  $$s_{yy} = \int y^2 \, ds \qquad v_{yy} = \int y^2 \, dv = \int xy \, dq$$  $$s_{xy} = \int xy \, ds$$  With reference to uniform loads:  $$w_x = + \int (\bar{x}' - x) l \, ds \qquad w_y = - \int (\bar{y}' - y) l \, ds$$  $$w_{ux} = + \int y(\bar{y}' - y) l \, ds \qquad w_{ux} = + \int x(\bar{y}' - y) l \, dr$$  $$w_{vx} = - \int x(\bar{x}' - x) l \, ds \qquad w_{vx} = - \int y(\bar{x}' - x) l \, dr$$  $$w_x = - \int (\bar{x}' - x) l \, du + \int (\bar{y}' - y) l \, dq$$  $$w_y = - \int (\bar{y}' - y) l \, dv - \int (\bar{x}' - x) l \, dq$$  $$w_{ux} = -\int x(\bar{x}' - x) l \, du + \int y(\bar{y}' - x) l \, dq$$  $$\qquad - \int y(\bar{y}' - y) l \, dv + \int x(\bar{y}' - y) l \, dq \quad (A.5)$$  When the equations (formulas A.4) are expressed in terms of the shape coefficients (formulas A.5) and the coefficients are presented in tabular form under their respective unknowns, the results appear as shown in Table A.1.

Text: By referring to the origin the moments and deflections at the free end in accordance with the following transfer formulas, the simplified form shown in Table A.2 is obtained.  $$M'_x = M_x + F_y z_A - F_z y_A$$  $$M'_y = M_y + F_z x_A - F_x z_A \quad (A.6)$$  $$M'_z = M_z + F_x y_A - F_y x_A$$  $$\delta^*_x = \delta_x + y_A \theta_z - z_A \theta_y$$  $$\delta^*_y = \delta_y + z_A \theta_x - x_A \theta_z \quad (A.7)$$  $$\delta^*_z = \delta_z + x_A \theta_y - y_A \theta_x$$  Note that each of the columns headed by $w_xL$, $w_yL$, and $w_zL$ in Table A.1 has been divided into two, the first two columns representing the moment at the origin due to the accumulated load, and the last column giving that load. By this arrangement the recurrence of the shape coefficients can easily be observed in each column having moments and forces with the same subscripts.  ---  HISTORY AND DERIVATION OF PIPING FLEXIBILITY ANALYSIS 307  The $x$-coordinate appearing under some of the integral signs in Table A.1 is that of any point of the member to the origin. As the line is assigned to the $y$-plane, $x$ is a constant equal to the distance of this plane from the origin. In Table A.2 the constant $x$ has been replaced by $c_x$ to indicate its true significance. Tables A.1 and A.2 cover only the coefficients for members in the $z$-plane. The corresponding coefficients for members in the $x$-plane or the $y$-plane can be similarly derived or can be readily obtained by cyclic permutation.  In the foregoing derivation the rotations and the deflections have been visualized as taking place at the free end $A$, the end $O'$ being fixed. These rotations and deflections may also be regarded as the differences between deformations at the free end and those at the fixed end and expressed as follows:  ![Fig. A.3 Auxiliary coordinate system used in integration of shape coefficients.](figures/MWK_1956_p0307_fig01_fig-a-3-auxiliary-coordinate-system-used.png)  $$\theta_x = \theta_{xA} - \theta_{xO'}$$ $$\theta_y = \theta_{yA} - \theta_{yO'}$$ $$\theta_z = \theta_{zA} - \theta_{zO'}$$ $$\delta^*_x = \delta^*_{xA} - \delta^*_{xO'} = \delta_{xA} + y_A\theta_{zA} - z_A\theta_{yA} - (\delta_{xO'} + y_O'\theta_{zO'} - z_O'\theta_{yO'}) \quad (A.8)$$ $$\delta^*_y = \delta^*_{yA} - \delta^*_{yO'} = \delta_{yA} + z_A\theta_{xA} - x_A\theta_{zA} - (\delta_{yO'} + z_O'\theta_{xO'} - x_O'\theta_{zO'})$$ $$\delta^*_z = \delta^*_{zA} - \delta^*_{zO'} = \delta_{zA} + x_A\theta_{yA} - y_A\theta_{xA} - (\delta_{zO'} + x_O'\theta_{yO'} - y_O'\theta_{xO'})$$  Consider next the pipe line $AB$ which lies in the $y$-plane as shown in Fig. A.2 and which is a continuation of the line $O'A$ of Fig. A.1. Designating the end $A$ fixed and the end $B$ free, the constant terms of the equations would be:  $$\theta_x = \theta_{xB} - \theta_{xA} \qquad \delta^*_x = \delta^*_{xB} - \delta^*_{xA}$$ $$\theta_y = \theta_{yB} - \theta_{yA} \qquad \delta^*_y = \delta^*_{yB} - \delta^*_{yA} \quad (A.9)$$ $$\theta_z = \theta_{zB} - \theta_{zA} \qquad \delta^*_z = \delta^*_{zB} - \delta^*_{zA}$$  For the combined configuration $O'B$, the difference in deformation between the ends $O'$ and $B$ would simply be the sum of the deformations of the partial configurations, $O'A$ and $AB$.  $$\theta_x = \theta_{xA} - \theta_{xO'} + \theta_{xB} - \theta_{xA} = \theta_{xB} - \theta_{xO'}, \text{ etc.} \quad (A.10)$$  Hence, the system of equations expressing the deformation differences between $O'$ and $B$ can be found by *adding the systems of equations for the partial configurations*. In a like manner it can be seen that similar operations may be performed for partial configurations in the $x$-plane.  Addition of the equations consists of adding the coefficients of the respective terms as indicated in Table A.3. The summation coefficients $A_{xx}$, $A_{xy}$, etc. thus determined are coefficients of a system of equations. If the integrals are evaluated for each of three shapes taking dimensions, locations, and orientations as variables, sets of formulas are obtained which permit the various shape coefficients or members to be computed by simple substitution. Shape coefficients for a group of members are simply summations of those for the individual members.  Since the principle of cyclic permutation permits ready transformation of formulas from one plane to another, the integrations for concentrated loads* are presented only for members in the $z$-plane. The integrations are simplified by using an auxiliary coordinate system $x'$, $y'$, as shown in Fig. A.3 which indicates the following relationships:  $$x = a + x'$$ $$y = b + y' \quad (A.11)$$

However, even for a very small value of $\tau$ (say a very small pressure drop across orifice), the magnification factor still tends to zero if the resonator frequency is *chosen so as to coincide with the forcing frequency $\omega$*. This then is the "tuning" phenomenon.  Since an ideal case is considered, the M.F. drops to zero at the tuning frequency. In a physical case this will not happen, of course, although in the neighborhood of the tuned frequency, the M.F. will drop sharply. The effect of the orifice pressure drop and resonator capacity, as reflected via the time constant $\tau$, is to maintain a lower value of the magnification factor in a *band* of frequencies around the tuned frequency; the larger $\tau$ the wider the band. If there exists no orifice, then instead of a concentrated pressure drop there will be a continuous pressure drop due to pipe friction. The smoothing will then occur in a finite length of pipe in the neighborhood of the resonator. Text: $Q_2(t)$ = mass flow rate from tank into piping system, time variable, slugs/sec.  $p(t)$ = pressure in tank, time variable, lbs/ft$^2$.  $p_0$ = pressure in pipe, considered constant, lbs/ft$^2$.  If smoothing is to be effective then the assumption that $p_0$ is constant will be valid.  $\rho(t)$ = density in tank, time variable, slugs/ft.  $T$ = temperature of gas in tank, degrees Rankine.  An *isothermal* process is assumed so that $T$ is constant.  $C$ = speed of sound, constant for an isothermal process, ft/sec.  $\bar{R}$ = gas constant, ft·lb/slugs $\times$ degrees F.  $\gamma$ = ratio of specific heats.  $$C = \sqrt{\gamma \bar{R} T} \quad (B.27)$$  It is assumed that the pressure drop across the effective orifice is moderate so that, at all times, the flow is well in the subsonic range. In this case, instead of the theoretically exact, but cumbersome, relation between pressure drop and flow rate through an orifice in the subsonic case, an approximate but simpler version of the Bernoulli type may be written:  $$Q_2(t) = a\sqrt{\rho(t)[p(t) - p_0]} \quad (B.28)$$  where $a$ = effective orifice area, including contraction coefficient, $\times \sqrt{2}$.  Then, by virtue of the gas law,  $$p = \bar{R}\rho T \quad (B.29)$$  and the definition of speed of sound $C$, eq. B.27,  $$Q_2(t) = \frac{a\sqrt{\gamma}}{C}\sqrt{p(t)[p(t) - p_0]} \quad (B.30)$$  From continuity:  $$Q_1(t) - Q_2(t) = V\dot{\rho}(t) \quad (B.31)$$  $$(\dot{\rho} = d\rho/dt)$$  But, on the assumption of an isothermal process,  $$\dot{\rho}(t) = \frac{\dot{p}(t)}{\bar{R}T} = \frac{\gamma}{C^2}\dot{p}(t) \quad (B.32)$$  Substituting the last result into eq. B.31 gives:  $$Q_1(t) - Q_2(t) = \frac{\gamma V}{C^2}\dot{p}(t) \quad (B.33)$$  ---  Substituting now the expression for $Q_2(t)$ from eq. B.30 into eq. B.33 and dividing through by a factor yields the following:  $$\dot{p}(t) + \frac{aC}{\gamma V} \sqrt{p(t)[p(t) - p_0]} = \frac{C^2}{\gamma V} Q_1(t) \quad (B.34)$$  $Q_1(t)$, being the output from the compressor, is a known time function. Hence, eq. B.34 is a first order differential equation for the instantaneous tank pressure $p(t)$. This differential equation, however, is non-linear.  It is supposed now that the pulsations are moderate in amplitude relative to their average values. Let the average values, being time independent, be represented by bars above the corresponding symbols. Thus:  $$p(t) = \bar{p} + \Delta p; \quad \dot{p}(t) = \Delta \dot{p} = d(\Delta p)/dt$$ $$Q_1(t) = \bar{Q}_1 + \Delta Q_1 = \bar{Q}_1 + \Delta Q_1$$

B.34 reduces, after some simplification, to:  $$\frac{\gamma V}{C^2} \bar{Q}_1 \left(\frac{\Delta \dot{p}}{\bar{p}}\right) + \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - p_0/\bar{p}} \cdot \frac{\Delta p}{\bar{p}} = \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} \quad (B.37)$$  Likewise, by virtue of eq. B.37 gives:  $$\frac{\gamma V}{C^2} \bar{Q}_1 \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} \left(\frac{\Delta \dot{Q}_2}{\bar{Q}_2}\right) + \frac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}_2} = \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} \quad (B.39)$$  Equation B.39 is a first order *linear* differential equation expressing the variation in outflow as a function of the variation in inflow (i.e. into the tank), relative to average values. If:  Inflow variation with respect to mean flow rate $\quad \dfrac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} = x$  Outflow variation with respect to mean flow rate $\quad \dfrac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}_2} = y$  Time contact $\quad \dfrac{\gamma V}{C^2} \dfrac{\bar{Q}_1}{\bar{p}} \dfrac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} = \tau$  $$(B.40)$$  then eq. B.39 assumes the form:  $$\tau \dot{y} + y = x \quad (B.41)$$  The last first order linear non-homogeneous differential equation is the familiar differential equation of a first order filter, $\tau$ being the "time constant" of the filter, having the dimension of time.  Since,  $$C^2 = \gamma \bar{R} \bar{T} = \frac{\gamma \bar{p}}{\bar{\rho}}$$

MacWatt *Sales Manager* *Power Piping Department* --- ## 5A-1 Introduction THE Kellogg general analytical method for relating the expansion displacements of space piping systems to terminal and intermediate forces, moments, and stresses was organized for internal company use in the early 1930's, was formally published in 1941 in the First Edition of the "Design of Piping Systems." In the Second Edition of the "Design of Piping Systems," published in 1956, the presentation was extended to include the combined effects of terminal and intermediate restraints, and of concentrated and distributed loads. This Second Edition also provided the mathematical basis for the simplification of complex problems by the inversion method, and a brief discussion of the then current application of computing machines.

Title: THE M. W. KELLOGG COMPANY
Text: In recent years, rapid developments in the field of digital computers have permitted the solution of increasingly complex piping systems with economy and versatility, not previously attainable. Although exploratory computer solutions were carried out much earlier, routine solutions were first obtained by Kellogg in 1954 using card programmed computing equipment. The magnetic drum type computer obtained in 1956 reduced computation time to one-tenth. The magnetic core type computer acquired by Kellogg in 1961 has further reduced computation time by still another factor of ten. With speed of this order, the ultimate objective of completely automatic machine analysis of arbitrarily complex piping systems has become a reality.

Title: Piping Flexibility and Stress Analysis
Text: With the development of computer programs of ever widening scope, the task of the program planner has become more demanding. The program must be so planned that any conceivable configuration can be analyzed, regardless of the number of branches, anchors, stops, or internal multiple closed loops. The program should require a minimum amount of input data and provide a maximum amount of automation. Essential to the attainment of these objectives is a rigorous statement of the computational problem in concise mathematical terms. The importance of this is attested by the growing acceptance of the notation of matrix algebra in the description of the piping problem. In recent years, Kellogg engineers and mathematicians have used vector and matrix algebra in re-deriving the shape coefficients for spatial pipes of any orientation and securing efficient solutions to piping problems of any complexity. This chapter summarizes the current Kellogg approach.

It will be shown that the shape coefficient matrix can be expressed as a function of two submatrices, one of which refers only to a local origin and a local coordinate system and, hence, is independent of the skewness of the member with respect to the common coordinate system chosen for the entire piping system. The other matrix serves to transfer the local coordinates to the common coordinate system, and is independent of the geometrical configuration of the pipe element, whether it be straight or curved. Following the theoretical derivation, the shape coefficient matrices for straight pipes and circular bends will be constructed, and a method of obtaining these matrices from minimal input data will be given.

The Shape Coefficient Matrix.  In piping analyses, it is convenient to consider a complex piping system, consisting of straight and curved members randomly oriented in space to be a cantilever (or a series of cantilevers), rigidly fixed at one end and free at the other (or others) upon which the redundant forces $\bar{F}$ and moments $\bar{M}$ act to preserve the prescribed physical conditions. These redundant forces and moments and the corresponding displacements are functions of the coordinates of the points of application. To facilitate analyses, it is customary to consider all the redundant forces and moments, and the corresponding displacements, to occur at a common origin and in the fixed $x$-system.  In what follows, we shall develop the shape coefficient matrix for a two-anchor system subject to thermal expansion. The generalization of this development to multiple anchor and loop problems will be discussed in Sec. 5A.3. We define:

Upon substitution of Eq. 5A.26 in the matrices of Eq. 5A.25, we get:  $$ |W_{jk}| = L'BL, $$ $$ |U_{jk}| = L'CL + N'BN + N'DL + L'D'N, \quad (5A.27) $$ $$ |V_{jk}| = L'BN + L'DL. $$  ---  Substituting Eq. 5A.27 in matrix $A$ which is defined in Eq. 5A.18, it is easy to verify that:  $$A = \begin{vmatrix} L' & O \\ N' & L' \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} B & D \\ D' & C \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} L & N \\ O & L \end{vmatrix} \quad (5A.28)$$  where $O$ represents a $3 \times 3$ null matrix. If we let:  $$X = \begin{vmatrix} B & D \\ D' & C \end{vmatrix}$$  $$Y = \begin{vmatrix} L & N \\ O & L \end{vmatrix} \quad (5A.29)$$  be the submatrices of the matrix $A$, Eq. 5A.28 can then be written as:  $$A = Y'XY \quad (5A.30)$$  The following observations may be made on the submatrices in Eq. 5A.30:  1. The $3 \times 3$ matrices $B$, $C$, and $D$ (Eq. 5A.26) in $X$ matrix have identical meanings in the $\lambda$-system as $|W_{ij}|$, $|U_{jl}|$ and $|V_{il}|$ (Eq. 5A.13) in the $x$-system. In fact, if the local origin is taken as the common origin, and the $\lambda$-system identical to the $x$-system, $N$ would become a null matrix as can be seen from Eqs. 5A.21 and 5A.26, and $L$ would become a diagonal unit matrix as can be seen from Eqs. 5A.3 and 5A.26. Consequently, $A$ simply becomes $X$. Therefore, $X$ may be called the shape coefficient matrix, but referred to the $\lambda$-system. It is implicit here that $X$ can be computed for every segment of a pipe irrespective of the $x$-system.  2. The $\lambda$-system, or the coordinates at the local origin, can be chosen so as to make the construction of the $X$ matrix as simple as possible. The correct choice of the $\lambda$-system for common piping configurations is not difficult to obtain as will be demonstrated in the illustrative examples in Section 5A-2.4.  3. The $Y$ matrix, consisting of terms which are functions of the position vector $\bar{q}$ and the local coordinate $\bar{\lambda}_i$ only, can be computed for every piping segment irrespective of its geometrical configuration. Once $\bar{q}$ and $\bar{\lambda}_i$ are given in the $x$-system, $Y$ follows from Eq. 5A.29.  When matrix $A$ becomes available for every segment of the pipe, the shape coefficient matrix for the entire pipe may be obtained by summation. Equation 5A.18 can again be used to obtain the redundants and Eq. 5A.19 the internal forces at any point along the pipe, except that $\alpha_{ij}$, $\beta_{ij}$ are now defined by Eq. 5A.24.  ## 4. Illustrative Examples  **a. Straight pipe (Figure 5A.2).** A straight pipe is chosen at the mid-point. The $\lambda$-system and $\bar{\xi}$-system are defined as shown. The systems are chosen such that each axis will coincide with the proper principal axis of the pipe.  Let the length $q\bar{p}$ be denoted as $s$. With respect to the $\lambda$-system, the following vectors with components in the 1, 2, and 3 directions listed in parentheses are first determined:  $$\bar{p} \quad (s, \; 0, \; 0)$$  $$\bar{\xi}_1 \quad (1, \; 0, \; 0)$$  $$\bar{\xi}_2 \quad (0, \; 1, \; 0)$$  $$\bar{\xi}_3 \quad (0, \; 0, \; 1)$$  $$\bar{e}_1 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_1 \quad (0, \; 0, \; 0)$$  $$\bar{e}_2 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_2 \quad (0, \; 0, \; s)$$  $$\bar{e}_3 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_3 \quad (0, \; -s, \; 0)$$  Then, following Eq. 5A.26, the submatrices $B$ and $D$ can be computed as follows:  $$B = |B_{rt}| = \sum_i b_i \int_{-l/2}^{l/2} \bar{\xi}_{ri} \bar{\xi}_{ti} \, ds$$  $$= \int_{-l/2}^{l/2} \sum_i b_i \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} ds$$  $$= \begin{vmatrix} b_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b_2 l & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_3 l \end{vmatrix}$$  ![Figure 5A.2](figures/MWK_1956_p0367_fig01_figure-5a-2.png)  ---  ## A MATRIX METHOD OF PIPING ANALYSIS AND USE OF DIGITAL COMPUTERS  $$ \begin{aligned} C &= \left| \sum_i a_i \int \xi_{i\epsilon} \xi_{i1} \, ds + \sum_i b_i \int \epsilon_{i\epsilon} \epsilon_{i1} \, ds \right| \\ &= \left| \begin{matrix} a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a_2 l & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a_3 l \end{matrix} \right| + \left| \begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12} \end{matrix} \right| \\ &= \left| \begin{matrix} a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a_2 l + \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a_3 l + \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12} \end{matrix} \right| \end{aligned} $$  $D = |0|.$  The matrix $X$ takes the following form:  $$ X = \left| \begin{matrix} b_1 l & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b_2 l & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_3 l & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & a_2 l + \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & a_3 l + \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12} \end{matrix} \right| $$  b. *Circular Bend* (Figure 5A.3). The $\lambda$ and $\bar{\xi}$-systems are chosen as shown, $\bar{\lambda}_3$ being parallel to the chord of the circular arc and $\bar{\lambda}_2$ directed toward the center of the bend, $Q$; whereas $\bar{\xi}_1$ is tangent to the arc in the increasing direction of the arc length and $\bar{\xi}_3$ is directed toward point $q$.  ![Figure 5A.3](figures/MWK_1956_p0368_fig01_figure-5a-3.png)  Let the arc length $QP$ be denoted as $s$. Then the following vectors can be specified in the $\lambda$-system:  $$ \begin{aligned} \bar{p} &\left( R \sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad R \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\ \bar{\xi}_1 &\left( \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad -\sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\ \bar{\xi}_2 &\left( -\sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad -\cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\ \bar{\xi}_3 &(0, \quad 0, \quad -1). \end{aligned} $$  It follows that:  $$ \begin{aligned} \bar{e}_1 &\left( 0, \quad 0, \quad -R \right), \\ \bar{e}_2 &\left( 0, \quad 0, \quad 0 \right), \\ \bar{e}_3 &\left( -R \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad R \sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right). \end{aligned} $$  Equation 5A.26 gives:  $$ B = \int_{-\frac{R\theta}{2}}^{\frac{R\theta}{2}} \left| \begin{matrix} \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & -\sin \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ -\sin \dfrac{s}{R} & -\cos \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{matrix} \right| \cdot \left| \begin{matrix} b_1 \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & -b_1 \sin \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ -b_2 \sin \dfrac{s}{R} & b_2 \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -b_3 \end{matrix} \right| ds $$  $$ = \left| \begin{matrix} \dfrac{R}{2} (b_1 \psi_1 + b_2 \psi_2) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{R}{2} (b_1 \psi_2 + b_2 \psi_1) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_3 R \theta \end{matrix} \right| $$  where  $$ \psi_1 = \theta + \sin \theta, \qquad \psi_2 = \theta - \sin \theta. \tag{a} $$  ---

Upon substitution of Eq. 5A.33, Eq. 5A.32 becomes:  $$EI \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}^{1} \\ \bar{a}^{2} \\ \bar{a}^{3} \\ \bar{a}^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{8} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{6} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{P_8} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^{8} \\ \bar{F}^{6} \\ \bar{F}^{4} \\ \bar{F}^{88} \end{vmatrix}$$  Since from Eq. 5A.34, $K_{08} K'_{80} = I$, the last equation may be modified as follows:  $$EI \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}^{1} \\ \bar{a}^{2} \\ \bar{a}^{3} \\ \bar{a}^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{8} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{6} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{P_8} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^{8} \\ \bar{F}^{6} \\ \bar{F}^{4} \\ \bar{F}^{88} \end{vmatrix}$$  (5A.35)  Equation 5A.35 is applicable to cases having orthogonal rigid stops whose directions coincide with the directions of the chosen coordinate axes. For orthogonal elastic stops, we must include the effects of elastic  ---  $$ EI \begin{vmatrix} \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \alpha^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^1 + A^2 + A^4 + A^5 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & (A^2 + A^4)K_{15} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^3 + A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4K_{56} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & (A^4 + A^6)K_{56} \\ K'_{15}(A^2 + A^4) & K'_{56}A^4 & K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6) & K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6)K_{56} + A^x \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} F^a \\ F^a \\ F^a \\ F^{aa} \end{vmatrix} $$  (5A.36)  where $A^* = \text{diag.} \, [1/x_1, 1/x_2, 1/x_3, 1/x_4, 1/x_5, 1/x_6]$, and $x_p$ ($p = 1, \ldots, 6$) are spring constants of moments and forces for the orthogonal elastic stops.  In the case of a skew force-stop which has direction cosines with the fixed coordinate axes as $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$, Eq. 5A.36 will be modified to be:  $$ EI \begin{vmatrix} \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \alpha_{\text{skew}} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^1 + A^2 + A^4 + A^5 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & (A^2 + A^4)K_{15}\overline{\beta} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^3 + A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4K_{56}\overline{\beta} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & (A^4 + A^6)K_{56}\overline{\beta} \\ \overline{\beta}^T K'_{15}A^4 & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}A^4 & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6) & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6)K_{56} + A^x\overline{\beta} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} F^a \\ F^a \\ F^a \\ F_{\text{skew}} \end{vmatrix} $$  (5A.37)  where $F_{\text{skew}}$ is the skew force and $\alpha_{\text{skew}}$ the skew displacement. They bear the following relationships with $\overline{F}^{88}$ and $\alpha^{88}$:  $$ F_{\text{skew}} = \overline{F}^{88}, \quad (5A.38) $$ $$ \alpha_{\text{skew}} = \overline{\beta}^T \alpha^{88}, $$  where  $$ \overline{\beta}^T = [0, 0, 0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3]. \quad (5A.39) $$  ## 5A-4 An Example  Figure 5A.9 shows a sketch of a reactor coolant loop representing a piping system with two anchors, one closed loop, and four elastic stops. Thus, a total of sixteen unknown moments and forces has to be determined.  Page 375 shows the input to the machine. By using the table marked "Key to Input Data", the input is self-explanatory. It should be noted that the flexibility factor (k) and the stress intensification factor (i) for curved members are automatically calculated if not specified.  Page 375 also shows the check of coordinates of the end points of each branch.  Page 376 (at top) shows the restraining moments and forces on anchors and stops as well as on additional points specified on the SUM-line on the input sheet A. The total actions on the anchor at the reactor are obtained by adding those for points 1 and 101. The maximum stress in the system is also automatically recorded.  Page 376 also gives the stresses, moments, deflections and rotations at each point of the system. Since a curved member in the input is denoted by a radius only, the machine calculates the tangent points which are indicated as A and B.  Finally page 377 gives the moments, forces and coordinates referred to the origin at the anchors, stops and intersections. These moments and forces are actually those from the solution of the equations. A complete print-out of the equations and the inversion of the same may be obtained by substituting an IND-card for an END-card. Utilizing this device, it is possible to split a complicated piping system into two or more parts if the capacity of the machine is insufficient to solve the required number of equations.  ---  ![FIGURE 5A.9](figures/MWK_1956_p0374_fig01_figure-5a-9.png)  ---  DESIGN OF PIPING SYSTEMS  ## THE M.
